paras: The lynching of John Dennis was the hanging of a Black man, also reported as Robert Denis or Robert Dennis, by a mob in Greenville, Washington County, Mississippi, on the afternoon of June 4, 1903. Accused of attempting to assault a white woman who worked at the telephone exchange, he was taken from the county jail and hanged in front of the exchange before hundreds of onlookers. Northern papers seized on a baseball game postponed so the crowd could watch, and J. K. Vardaman later praised the lynching while campaigning in Mississippi.

According to the wire report, the attempt occurred the previous Tuesday night as the young woman walked home from the exchange, and he was arrested at once. A Greenville dispatch in the Hattiesburg Daily Progress placed it on Monday night and named her Miss Bishop; the Weekly Corinthian called her Miss Beulah Bishop. The New York Sun added that he had been given a preliminary hearing and bound over to court, and the Hattiesburg dispatch said officers had stopped "attempt after attempt" to seize him.

At about four o'clock on Thursday a body of men, 200 by the wire and about 100 by the Hattiesburg dispatch, were refused admittance at the jail. They battered a side door with a timber and then an iron rail and broke into the cell, while Judge Kimbrough, holding court across the yard, pleaded in vain for the law to take its course. The city bell then struck three times, and within ten minutes about 700 people had gathered.

The prisoner was marched to the exchange on Washington Avenue by a crowd the Hattiesburg correspondent described as lawyers, doctors and merchants, "large, but orderly." A rope was thrown over a telephone cable, though the wire said he was hanged from a pole's cross-arm. He was allowed to pray, but when he asked to make a statement the crowd pulled him up. Black onlookers were told to take warning that "southern homes, honor and virtue must be protected."

Women watched from galleries, and The Sun put the crowd at more than 1,000 men, women and children. No shot was fired, no masks were worn, and the body was left hanging. Many then went to the ball park, where the game had been postponed forty minutes.

No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage. The Indianapolis Freeman, the Seattle Republican and The Leader listed the death, as Robert Dennis, in their June lynching tallies. Speaking at Crystal Springs, Vardaman thanked God the Greenville people "broke his neck"; the Meridian Press, reprinted in the Kemper Herald, condemned him, and the Hernando Times-Promoter revived the dispute in August.

On June 5 the wire report ran in the Montgomery, Savannah, Birmingham, Wichita and Wheeling dailies under headlines such as "MANY WOMEN SEE NEGRO LYNCHED." It stated the assault attempt as fact, and the Watertown Republican headed it "Colored Brute Taken from Jail."

Mississippi papers were openly approving. The Hattiesburg Daily Progress headlined "SWIFT DEATH METED OUT TO NEGRO FIEND," called him a "savage in the form of a negro," and joked editorially that in praying he "wanted to send a long distance message over the wires." A Christian Advocate editorial in the Lexington Progress-Advertiser, on an unnamed Mississippi hanging where "not a shot was fired," called such a lynching "unjustifiable."

Northern editors fixed on the ball game. The Sun headlined "GAME DELAYED FOR LYNCHING," the Evening World's "Southern Amusements" said Greenville "started for a baseball game on Thursday and landed at a lynching" while granting that the crime deserved death, and the Redwood Gazette called it an "every day incident" in the South.

No Black-press news report was found. On June 20 the Colored American reprinted a paragraph from The Progress denouncing the Greenville "blood suckers" and calling the accusation "a lie," asserting without evidence that the woman was "only his mistress"; the Freeman and Seattle Republican listed the death only in their tallies.

The wire and Hattiesburg dispatch named him John Dennis, The Sun Robert Denis, and the Corinthian and tallies Robert Dennis. Early reports described an attempted assault, later Mississippi items an assault, and the Colored American paragraph denied the charge.

reader.title: Lynching of John Dennis
bases: A crowd broke into the Washington County jail, took out a Black prisoner accused of attempted assault and hanged him in the street (A3, A11, A16).

Every account says a mob of 100 to 200 men took the accused man from jail against a judge's plea and hanged him for an alleged attempted assault on a white woman (A3, A11, A16, A2); the Hattiesburg dispatch framed it as protecting 'southern homes, honor and virtue' (A12).

The wire report (A3), a separate New York dispatch (A2), a long Greenville dispatch (A11, A12) and a second Mississippi dispatch (A16) agree on the jail break and hanging, and Black and white lynching tallies list the death (A25, A26, A30).

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A mob of 200 battered down the jail door with a railway rail and hanged John Dennis on the cross-arm of a telephone pole at the exchange for an attempted assault on a young woman on Tuesday night; many women watched and he asked only time to pray.

accounts.label: New York dispatch (The Sun)
accounts.gist: Robert Denis had been bound over after a preliminary hearing when the mob broke in, hanged him to a telephone cable before more than 1,000 people, and went on to a ball game postponed forty minutes for the hanging.

accounts.label: Greenville dispatch (Hattiesburg Daily Progress)
accounts.gist: About 100 men broke the side door and cell after officers had repeatedly interfered, ignored Judge Kimbrough's plea, marched him to the exchange where his accuser Miss Bishop worked, and hanged him over a cable; no shot was fired and the body was left hanging.

accounts.label: Greenville dispatch (Weekly Corinthian)
accounts.gist: Two hundred citizens broke the rear door and cell bars, took Robert Dennis, accused of attempting to assault Miss Beulah Bishop, and hanged him over a cable wire in front of the exchange; no masks were worn.

accounts.label: The Progress, via the Colored American
accounts.gist: The accusation was 'a lie'; the woman was 'only his mistress' and he died for being caught with her.

framing.detail: The Hattiesburg Daily Progress headlined 'SWIFT DEATH METED OUT TO NEGRO FIEND', called him a 'brute' and 'savage in the form of a negro', and joked on its editorial page about a 'long distance message'.
Southern and midwestern dailies ran the wire report under headlines such as 'MANY WOMEN SEE NEGRO LYNCHED' and 'Colored Brute Taken from Jail', stating the assault attempt as fact.
The Sun, the Evening World and the Redwood Gazette mocked the delayed ball game, though the Evening World said the man's crime deserved death.

A Christian Advocate editorial reprinted in Lexington, Miss., called an unnamed Mississippi lynching of this kind 'unjustifiable' while saying it expressed the people's determination to avenge a crime.
The Meridian Press, reprinted in the Kemper Herald, attacked Vardaman for praising the Greenville lynching.
The Colored American reprinted The Progress denouncing the Greenville 'blood suckers' and calling the accusation a lie.
